**Florida city cancels St. Patrick's Day parade, citing new anti-DEI law: NPR**
Delray Beach, Florida, canceled its St. Patrick's Day parade after a nearly 60-year run, citing a new state law that prohibits taxpayer dollars from going toward diversity initiatives. Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-6041093/st-patricks-day-parade-canceled-florida-dei)

**New Mexico wanted free childcare for all. This is what's worked — and what hasn't: NPR**
A year ago in November, New Mexico became the first state to offer free childcare to every eligible family, regardless of income. Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/15/nx-s1-6040194/new-mexico-free-universal-childcare-families)

**A new generation of disability rights activists carry on Judy Heumann's legacy: NPR**
The film Being Heumann, premiering November 13, 2026, on Apple TV, tells the lesser-known story of Judy Heumann, described as the mother of the disability rights movement, while a new generation of activists say they are carrying that work forward. Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/15/nx-s1-6002935/being-heumann-new-generation-disability-rights)

**FAA ground stop disrupts college football: NPR**
Some college football games were delayed a few hours on Saturday or postponed to Sunday after the nationwide ground stop, and in Oklahoma fans were offered perks including cheap beers to make up for the inconvenience. Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-6041115/faa-ground-stop-college-football-delays)

### The Region and the World
**Europe and NATO will determine their own security, not Russia - Canadian Prime Minister Carney: Censor**
Prime Minister Mark Carney told journalists that the security architecture of a free Europe will be determined by a free Europe and NATO, not by Russia or the revised Minsk agreements, Censor.NET reported, citing Ukrinform. He said decisions on the security of a free Europe should be made by European countries themselves, together with NATO, and that Canada will continue to support its allies and will not leave other Alliance members without support. About 2,500 Canadian troops are stationed in Latvia, where Canada leads a NATO multinational brigade. Commenting on Russia's demand that NATO troops be withdrawn from the Baltic states and Poland, Carney said Russia will not get a cordon sanitaire, adding, "Everyone knows how 'well' that idea worked in the 1940s." Censor.NET notes that "cordon sanitaire" is a geopolitical term for a system of states joined to create a barrier, coined by French Prime Minister Georges Clemenceau in 1919 in reference to the former Russian Empire. Source: [censor.net](https://censor.net/en/news/4033775/mark-carney-europe-and-nato-will-determine-the-security-architecture-themselves)

### Both Sides: Closing East Potomac Park for a championship golf course
Judge Ana C. Reyes of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia is weighing whether the Trump administration may close East Potomac Park in Washington, including its municipal golf course, in order to start work on a championship course. On Saturday she temporarily blocked the administration from shuttering the park. NPR reports that the order is a two-week delay to any work at the historic public course, not far from the White House. President Trump had announced that the municipal golf course and park would close on Sunday, ahead of renovation work he had called for. The Times reports that her ruling means the park will remain open for now.

President Trump's stated course is the renovation he called for. The New York Times reports he announced the Sunday closure ahead of transforming the area into a championship golf course, and Judge Reyes found that the proposed closure appeared intended to start that process.

Against closure, a preservationist organization and local golfers sued in February. Their argument, as the Times reports it, is that the project threatened to destroy a historic course that remained a cheap and accessible option for recreational players.

In a 30-page order, Judge Reyes said the Trump administration would not be responsible for operating the course while the case proceeded, and she required the golf courses, paths and picnic areas to remain open and accessible to the public. She has overseen the litigation for months, including a series of earlier rulings limited to whether the administration could clear trees at the site. Saturday's order was the first blocking work at the park more generally. The Times reports she has repeatedly accused administration officials of concealing their efforts to move forward with the president's plans. The Sunday closure does not proceed, and the courses, paths and picnic areas stay open to the public while the case goes on. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/politics/trump-east-potomac-golf-course.html) Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-6041152/judge-trump-golf-course-blocks)

**SpaceX successfully catches Starship and makes history: NPR**
SpaceX caught its Starship at the company's Texas launchpad: the spacecraft returned by carefully lowering itself until two metal arms attached to the launch tower secured it, NPR reports. A completed catch is a finished recovery of the vehicle on the pad, not an announcement of a future attempt. Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/g-s1-153786/spacex-successfully-catches-starship-and-makes-history)

episodes.episode_title: Ep 49: On his second China trip this year, Trump will not press Xi on the Huang spy finding.
episodes.content:
# Omni View North America
> **On his second China trip this year, Trump will not press Xi on the Huang spy finding.**

**What You Need to Know:** On his second China trip this year, President Trump is heading to Asia to meet Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, and he has indicated he will not press Xi about U.S. intelligence findings that a Chinese spy targeted Jensen Huang. NPR says Nvidia fallout hangs over the trip, and that it comes as the president and his party faced widespread voter backlash in the recent midterms. The New York Times is the outlet that reports the indicated decision not to raise that finding.

### Lead
**Nvidia Fallout Looms Over Trump-Xi Meeting: The New York Times**
President Trump is heading to Asia to meet China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin, a trip NPR says is shadowed by Nvidia fallout. The China stop is his second there this year. The New York Times reports that, so far, Trump has indicated he does not plan to press the Chinese leader about U.S. intelligence findings that a Chinese spy targeted Nvidia's Jensen Huang. NPR says the trip comes as the president and his party faced widespread backlash from voters in the recent midterm elections. What the two newsrooms put in front of the Xi meeting is that finding, and the president's indicated choice not to raise it with the Chinese leader while he is also set to meet Putin. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/politics/nvidia-trump-huang-china-xi.html) Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/16/nx-s1-6041738/trump-xi-and-putin-china-nvidia)

### Across the Region
**CBSA demoting border officers who permanently lost ability to use sidearm: CBC**
The Canada Border Services Agency has informed 63 employees that they will have to take on new, lower-paid positions because of medical conditions that prevent them from carrying a sidearm. CBC reports the move as a demotion of border officers who have permanently lost the ability to use that sidearm. The notices are an agency decision on firearm accommodation for those 63 employees. Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/cbsa-firearm-accommodation-medical-union-9.7421365?cmp=rss)

**As millions lose food aid nationwide, this SNAP office is doubling up as a food pantry: NPR**
Millions are losing food aid nationwide as cuts and changes hit SNAP, and a San Diego SNAP office is doubling as a food pantry. NPR reports that the cuts and changes have been difficult for government workers who take pride in helping others. In San Diego, those workers said they could not sit back while their neighbors went hungry. The office's second role is a local answer, by the people who administer the benefit, to a national reduction in food assistance. Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/16/nx-s1-6034048/snap-san-diego-food-assistance)

**Flight disruptions expected to last into Monday: NPR**
Flight disruptions are expected to last into Monday, NPR reports, after Friday's nationwide ground stop, and Congress has given the Department of Transportation $12.5 billion to upgrade the aging air traffic control system while President Trump wants more. The New York Times reports that operations are returning to normal after air traffic was shut down for more than four hours on Friday, following a maintenance upgrade that crippled communications. NPR's morning news brief says thousands of travelers are still waiting to reschedule flights after that ground stop. The money Congress has already provided, and the further sum the president wants, sit beside a system that is still clearing Friday's shutdown into the start of the week. Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/15/nx-s1-6041683/flight-disruptions-expected-to-last-into-monday) Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/faa-groundstop-flights-status-delays-canceled.html) Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/16/nx-s1-6038373/morning-news-brief)

### The Closer Look
**North Atlantic right whale population declines as U.S. weakens protections: The Globe and Mail**
The North Atlantic right whale population has slipped back into decline. The North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium, meeting in Halifax, released an estimate on Monday of about 382 animals at the end of 2025 — seven fewer than a year earlier, 20 percent below the most recent peak of 483 in 2011, and the end of four years of fragile growth. The species lost about a quarter of its numbers in less than a decade after that peak. Heather Pettis of the New England Aquarium, who chairs the consortium, said this population cannot afford another slide like that. Entanglements in fishing gear and vessel strikes remain the leading threats to animals that migrate between Canadian and U.S. waters to feed and give birth. Climate change has pushed the whales into new feeding grounds, and ocean noise adds to the pressure. Scientists say recovery depends on both countries, at a time when Pettis says their approaches are diverging. In the United States, she said, there are movements to deregulate and backslide on protective measures.

Congress has barred new rules for U.S. lobster and crab fisheries to prevent entanglement through 2028, and the House of Representatives has passed a bill, still awaiting Senate approval, to extend that pause to 2035. Pettis said that could stall talks on the next round of rules, and that a delay is the last thing needed. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is considering deregulatory action on its 2008 rule requiring large vessels to slow in seasonal right whale zones along the U.S. East Coast, including swapping speed limits for acoustic or other technology that detects whales and alerts ships in real time. NOAA Fisheries spokesperson John Chu said the 2008 rule remains in effect while the agency reviews public comments. Pettis said the new technology, while promising, is not ready to replace the vessel-speed rule — an "and," not an "or." A separate federal rule that came into effect on Sept. 14 narrows the definition of "harm" under the Endangered Species Act. Because right whale deaths are incidental, Pettis called that change cause for alarm, though the whales are still covered by the Marine Mammal Protection Act. Chu said the change targets unnecessary or duplicative permitting requirements for projects and industries, not protections, and that risk reduction must be a shared responsibility.

Canada, Pettis said, has been much more nimble, and Sean Brillant of the Canadian Wildlife Federation said that with the United States pulling back, Ottawa needs to hold or step up its efforts. Canada first brought in fishing closures and vessel speed limits after a wave of deaths in the Gulf of St. Lawrence in 2017. Brillant said that at best ended the nosedive, and that the species is still on a knife's edge. Two of the three whales found entangled with fishing gear this year were in the gulf, the most recent on Oct. 21, said Lindsey Jones, who manages the North Atlantic Right Whale Catalog at the New England Aquarium. In February, Fisheries and Oceans Canada rolled out its Whalesafe Fishing Gear Strategy, which aims to keep fishing areas open when right whales are present and allows harvesters to use on-demand, or ropeless, gear that keeps buoy lines on the sea floor until traps are hauled. Alexis Van Bemmel of the department said Canadian harvesters and industry have been the real leaders in testing it. After closures near North Lake, Prince Edward Island, and Cheticamp, Nova Scotia, the Canadian Wildlife Federation's CanFISH gear-lending program trained about 85 harvesters and deckhands, nearly as many as in all the years since 2022, and it was the first year lobster was landed commercially from a right whale closure in Canada. Lost gear is a separate problem: Division, number 5217 in the catalog, a four-year-old male found dead off North Carolina in January, was entangled in rope from a snow crab area in the southern Gulf of St. Lawrence that had not been fished in five years. Marina Petrovic of Fisheries and Oceans Canada said gear-marking rules let the department trace it. Since 2019, the department's ghost-gear program has removed more than 2,620 tonnes of lost fishing gear and more than 1,040 kilometres of rope, and a national ghost-gear action plan is expected next spring. The 2025-26 season also brought 24 calves, the fourth-highest on record. # Omni View North America
> **Nine years on, Canada and China revive a currency swap, easing tariffs for exporters.**

**What You Need to Know:** Nine years on, Canada and China are reviving a currency swap and easing tariffs, a shift for exporters who move goods between the two countries. In Shenzhen on Tuesday, President Xi Jinping and Prime Minister Mark Carney paired that relief with more flights and a wider cooperation list ahead of the Asia-Pacific leaders' meeting. Outlets also reported looser Canadian steel rules and wider Chinese access for pork.

### Lead
**Carney and Xi Announce Trade Pact Ahead of Asia Summit: The New York Times**
In Shenzhen on Tuesday, Chinese President Xi Jinping met Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who is in China for the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders' Meeting on November 18 and 19, Xinhua reported. The New York Times reported that the two announced a trade pact ahead of that summit. Anadolu Agency reported that China and Canada agreed to tariff relief. The South China Morning Post reported that the two sides will revive a bilateral currency swap after nine years. Yahoo Finance Canada reported that Xi is opening more pork access as Carney loosens steel restrictions. CBC reported partnerships on Carney's first full day in Shenzhen: an expansion of current tariff agreements, more flights between the two countries, and agreements covering education and the arts. Xi said improving the relationship is the right choice for both peoples and for world peace, stability, development and prosperity, and that China is ready to advance the new strategic partnership launched when the two met earlier this year. He said the countries should deepen cooperation in trade, energy, agriculture and finance, and expand it in the green economy, e-commerce and the digital economy. Carney said relations have been on the right track since that partnership began, and that Canada will pursue stronger cooperation in trade, investment, new energy, agricultural products, artificial intelligence and tourism, reduce the list of irritants and expand the list of cooperation. CFJC Today reported that Carney and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum are set to meet in China. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/17/world/canada/carney-china-xi-trade-apec.html) Source: [english.news.cn](https://english.news.cn/20261117/82d287569a714cf0906ad937760de732/c.html) Source: [aa.com.tr](https://www.aa.com.tr/en/politics/improvement-in-ties-right-choice-xi-tells-carney-as-china-canada-agree-to-tariff-relief/4127301) Source: [scmp.com](https://www.scmp.com/economy/article/3374743/china-and-canada-revive-bilateral-currency-swap-after-nine-years) Source: [ca.finance.yahoo.com](https://ca.finance.yahoo.com/news/carney-meets-president-xi-shenzhen-023952920.html) Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/canada-china-carney-xi-9.7424608?cmp=rss) Source: [cfjctoday.com](https://cfjctoday.com/2026/11/17/carney-and-sheinbaum-set-to-meet-in-china-as-both-countries-navigate-trumps-tumult/)

### Across the Region

The filing confirms the administration has pursued that identification on two parallel fronts. Those fronts are part of one overarching investigation. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/us/politics/trump-linkedin-data-nyt-sources.html)

**Victim Advocates Sue Newsom Over Attempt to Empty California’s Death Row: The New York Times**

The paper said Newsom is trying to spare the lives of 548 prisoners there. Prosecutors and victims' families say that amounts to an abuse of power. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/us/newsom-sued-death-penalty-commuations-california.html)

**Ford holds off on new cash for Stellantis plant, contradicting minister: Global News**

His minister responsible for the tariff response said the province is willing to offer Stellantis additional financial support to stay in Brampton. The premier's pause and the minister's offer are the two positions now on the record. Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12153708/ford-holds-off-on-new-cash-for-stellantis-plant-contradicting-minister/)

### The Closer Look
**After 7 years in Canada, young student faces deportation: Global News**
Students and faculty at Dawson College in Montreal are rallying around Luisa Juliana Chaves Munoz, a young student ordered to leave Canada with her family by the end of December. Global News reported that her classmates and teachers argue she should at least be allowed to finish her studies first. Munoz said the family received the deportation notice on October 15, seven years after they arrived. On Monday the campus launched a letter-writing campaign directed at several members of Parliament, hoping political pressure could help the family remain. The office of Brossard-St-Lambert MP Alexandra Mendès said it is working with the family and declined further details, citing privacy protocols.

Munoz said the family came from Colombia seeking asylum because of violence and death threats against her mother. The asylum claim was denied. She said she left as a child, no longer has ties to Colombia, and that her only childhood friend was killed as an indirect result of the violence there. "Now that she's gone, I would have to relive the whole thing," Munoz said about returning. The family applied for permanent residency on humanitarian grounds two years ago. Canada's immigration department said that application does not cancel a deportation order and would still be reviewed, a process that could take several years.

The stake for Munoz is a credential and money already paid. She said the family has spent $28,000 on tuition and that her courses are not transferable outside Quebec. Katz said completing her CEGEP studies would leave a recognized credential, while leaving before graduation would mean the work already completed would not amount to a degree. Teachers and fellow students called the handling of the deportation inhumane and questioned why she cannot remain long enough to finish. The order requires the family to leave by the end of December, the date the reporting gives as the deadline. Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12153885/canada-student-deportation-montreal-que-dawson/)

### The Region and the World
**Military's No. 2 defends GlobalEye surveillance jets despite capability concerns: CBC**
Vice-Admiral Angus Topshee, the Canadian military's second-in-command, told members of Parliament on Monday that he is satisfied with the procurement process for Saab's GlobalEye surveillance jets, CBC reported. He argued the aircraft will contribute to an integrated continental defence network. The defence comes despite capability concerns about the jets. Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/surveillance-jets-global-eye-canada-saab-9.7424260?cmp=rss)

### Both Sides: A religious-symbols ban for Quebec elementary students
Quebec's minority Parti Québécois government has proposed extending a ban on religious symbols to elementary school students, and it needs opposition votes to advance the plan. Conservative Leader Eric Duhaime has left the door open. He said his party is generally in favour of living in a secular society, and that the link with limits already placed on some public-sector workers is a wish to banish religious symbols in the public space, especially inside public institutions. He said Conservatives feel uneasy seeing a young girl arrive at school with a veil. He would not commit his party's votes. He said Conservatives want to know how a ban would be implemented, who would be responsible, and what the process would be, before they take a clear stand.

The Quebec Liberals and Québec solidaire have said they would vote against the proposal. Joe Ortona, chair of the English Montreal School Board, said legislating what children can wear would cross a line, and that the debate is pulling focus from real systemic problems in education. Harini Sivalinga of the Canadian Civil Liberties Association called the idea a new low and said people should be as outraged as the association that the government would go this far. Stephen Brown of the National Council of Canadian Muslims asked whether Quebec would deny children entry to math class over a turban or a kippah. The proposal would go further than the previous Coalition Avenir Québec ban on religious symbols for some public-sector workers, a law whose challenge has reached the Supreme Court. That court's decision on Bill 21 is expected in the coming weeks. Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12153880/quebec-conservatives-pq-religious-symbols-ban-children/)

The figure matters because birds taken out of trafficking are not only alive in care; in those two cases they have reproduced. episodes.content:
> **Democrats claim fifty-six Senate seats after Mary Peltola wins Alaska.**

# Omni View North America

**What You Need to Know:** Democrats claim fifty-six Senate seats after Mary Peltola wins Alaska, unseating two-term Senator Dan S. Sullivan and becoming the first Democrat to hold that seat since 2015. The Trump administration's SNAP changes require adults up to age 65 to work or volunteer for food aid. Waymo has pulled driverless taxis off U.S. freeways after California's motor-vehicle agency cited an imminent hazard.

### Lead
**Democrats Claim 56 Senate Seats After Mary Peltola Wins in Alaska: The New York Times**
The New York Times reports that Mary Peltola has defeated Senator Dan S. Sullivan in Alaska. Sullivan was a two-term incumbent. Peltola becomes the first Democrat to represent the state in the Senate since 2015. Democrats claim 56 Senate seats after the win. Axios reports that Alaska Native strongholds pushed Peltola into that Senate history. The change, as those accounts state it, is Alaska's seat and the Democratic claim of 56 seats. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/17/us/politics/alaska-senate-sullivan-peltola.html) · [axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2026/11/18/alaska-native-strongholds-peltola-senate-history)

### Across the Region
**She retired early to care for family. New work rules for food aid disrupted that: NPR**
NPR reports that the Trump administration's changes to SNAP mean older adults up to age 65 must work or volunteer to get the benefit. NPR describes the changes as sweeping. The account is of people who retired early to care for family and then met the new work rules. For adults through age 65, food aid is now tied to work or volunteering. Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/18/nx-s1-5954231/snap-work-rules-retirees)

**Waymo Pulls Its Driverless Taxis From All U.S. Freeways Temporarily: The New York Times**
The New York Times reports that Waymo has pulled its driverless taxis from all U.S. freeways temporarily. The move came after California's Department of Motor Vehicles ordered the cars off the state's freeways. The department cited an "imminent hazard to public safety." Freeway service stops nationwide for now, not only on California freeways. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/17/us/waymo-ban-california-freeway.html)

**Canada wants to get close to tariff-free trade in CUSMA talks: Charette: Global News**
Global News reports that Canada wants to get close to tariff-free trade in CUSMA talks, in comments from Charette. President Donald Trump said in July that the United States would not renew the CUSMA deal in its current form. That position, as Global News reports it, forces the deal to be reviewed annually. Canadian negotiators are taking a near-tariff-free aim into a review the U.S. president has already framed as a rejection of the current text. Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12155184/cusma-talks-tariff-free-trade-charette/)

### The Closer Look
**Carney pitches proposed Pacific Link crude pipeline to business leaders at Asian summit: The Globe and Mail**
Prime Minister Mark Carney on Wednesday pitched a proposed new oil pipeline to the West Coast at the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation CEO summit in Shenzhen. He said Canada is advancing Pacific Link, a pipeline to the Pacific that will carry an additional one million barrels a day to growing markets in Asia, diversifying trade and reinforcing Canada as a reliable energy partner for the region. The Globe and Mail reports crude oil exports to China hit $3.5-billion in the third quarter of 2026, up nearly 159 per cent from the same period a year earlier, according to the University of Alberta's China Institute. Volumes were nearly double the same 2025 period at about 327,000 barrels a day. Much of that flow, the paper reports, is due to extra capacity from the Trans Mountain expansion that began operating in 2024.

Ottawa said earlier this fall it would expedite federal approval for Pacific Link, a decision that is attracting legal challenges from numerous First Nations. At the start of October the federal government announced a national-interest designation for the line, from the Edmonton area to a port in the Vancouver region. That was the first such move under the Building Canada Act, which The Globe and Mail calls a centrepiece of Carney's work to shift Canada's economy away from the United States. The designation gives Ottawa's backing at the start and is meant to let the government grant many permits much more quickly than in the past. In Shenzhen, Carney pitched chief executives on clearing red tape from approvals for major resource and infrastructure projects. He said Canada, which for much of its history looked to the United States and Europe, is also looking to Asia.

He said that two years ago Canada had never shipped a major liquefied natural gas cargo to Asia, and that since LNG Canada's first shipment in June 2025 the country has shipped more than 11 million tonnes. He said Canada will quadruple that by the end of the decade and double it again in the next one. # Omni View North America

> **An eleven-point-eight-million-dollar tab of free work now ties Kirkland and Ellis to the Trump administration.**

**What You Need to Know:** Kirkland & Ellis has disclosed about 6,491 hours of free work, about $11.8 million, under the deal it reached with the Trump administration. Anthropic’s stock-market debut is being reported at record scale, and in Alaska Representative Nick Begich III has narrowly defeated an independent House challenger. In Canada, KPMG says client tax documents were accessed in a cyber breach, while Pfizer is stopping supply of a long-used menopause drug.

### Lead
**In Bending to Trump, Law Firm Did $11.8 Million of Free Work for Administration: The New York Times**
Kirkland & Ellis has quietly disclosed that, as part of the deal it reached with the Trump administration, it has done about 6,491 hours of free work. The New York Times puts the value of that work at $11.8 million. The hours are free work for the administration under that deal, not a separate contract announced as new law or a court order. The disclosure puts a dollar figure on legal work the firm is providing to the administration because of the deal. It is the firm’s own accounting, reported by the Times, of work already done. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/19/us/politics/kirkland-ellis-law-firm-trump.html)

### Across the Region
**AI giant Anthropic raises more than $100 billion in record-setting IPO: NPR**
Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, is entering the public market in a debut both the BBC and NPR describe as a record. The BBC reports that Anthropic raises $81 billion and will become one of the most valuable firms in the world. NPR reports that the company raises more than $100 billion, and that shares in the maker of Claude will start trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday. The two figures are each outlet’s account of the same debut, not a single reconciled total. What is settled in both reports is the event: a U.S. artificial-intelligence company is listing, and trading is set to begin Thursday. Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/19/nx-s1-6042558/anthropic-ipo-breaks-records-100-billion) Source: [bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6742m39xgzxo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

**Alaska Republican Narrowly Defeats Independent House Candidate: The New York Times**
Representative Nick Begich III, a Republican, has narrowly defeated an independent challenger for a U.S. House seat in Alaska. The New York Times reports that he overcame that independent in a year in which, the Times says, Democrats made historic gains but third-party candidates had little success. The result is a completed House race, not a projection. It keeps the seat with Begich after a contest the Times describes as narrow. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/us/politics/alaska-nick-begich-wins-house-race.html)

**KPMG Canada says client documents accessed in cybersecurity breach: Global News**
KPMG Canada says some client tax documents were accessed in a cybersecurity breach. The firm is reaching out to clients who were affected. Spokesperson Sonja Cloutier-Bosworth says the company is confident that the accessed data is not available online or being misused for any purpose. Global News describes it as the latest in a string of cyberattacks targeting organizations in Canada, including those in the legal and financial sectors. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security said in an alert last month that multiple firms had been targeted by people impersonating internal IT support and directing employees to fake sign-in pages. Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12157485/kpmg-canada-breach/)

### The Closer Look
**Menopause experts raise concerns after Pfizer discontinues drug in Canada: The Globe and Mail**
Pfizer is stopping supply of Premarin cream and Premarin oral estrogen tablets in Canada while continuing to offer them in the United States, and menopause specialists say Canadian patients will carry the consequences. The decision was made public last week. Existing inventory is expected to last until next year. Premarin was first developed and approved in Canada in 1941. Pfizer manufactures the global supply of the active ingredient in Brandon, Manitoba, from the urine of pregnant mares in Manitoba and Saskatchewan.

Pfizer first notified Health Canada on November 3 that it would stop supplying Premarin products, according to a federal drug-shortage database. The cream is being discontinued immediately. Pills will be available while inventory lasts, potentially until next June, the database notices say. Pfizer said the products were commercially unsustainable in Canada. Sophie Morin, a spokesperson for Pfizer Canada, said the company considered manufacturing and supply costs, the pricing and reimbursement environment, and the ability to maintain sustainable supply over the longer term. The federal database shows the cream has been in shortage four times since the beginning of 2025.

In the United States, demand for menopause hormone therapy has grown after the Food and Drug Administration initiated the removal of long-standing safety warnings on the treatments last November. Health Canada has not removed similar warnings on products in Canada. Demand is rising here as well. In September, a Manulife Canada report on its group benefits showed a 228 percent increase in hormone-replacement therapy claims over five years among women 45 to 54.

Canadian obstetrician-gynecologist Jen Gunter wrote on Wednesday on her blog that Pfizer’s decision should concern all Canadians, and that the issue is larger than one brand: people who care about access to medications should speak up. In cream form, Premarin applies estrogen directly to vaginal tissue. It is used to treat atrophic vaginitis, including drying of the vaginal walls and shrinkage of the skin of the vagina and vulva, and it can be used for dyspareunia, pain or discomfort during intercourse. Gunter wrote that some alternatives are available, but that Premarin may be better for some patients on side effects and efficacy. Physicians say stopping certain treatments can bring back hot flashes and vaginal irritation and can set patients back in their menopause care.

A tube of Premarin cream in Canada typically retails for around $50 because of federal drug rules, compared with around $400 to $500 in the United States. Some patients pay less if they have insurance. Rithvika Ramesh, a family physician in Toronto, said the discontinuation affects some of her patients. It is the only vaginal estrogen cream covered under the Ontario Drug Benefit program, which covers certain medications for eligible residents. She said the cream has long been used for genitourinary symptoms of menopause and to help prevent recurrent urinary tract infections. For older adults, she said, preventing those infections can be life-saving, because a seemingly uncomplicated infection can progress to a kidney infection, hospitalization, and sometimes sepsis — an extreme immune reaction that can shut organs down and, in some cases, lead to death. She said access to effective vaginal estrogen is not only a quality-of-life question but a part of preventive care.

Lily Barnes, a spokesperson for Ontario Health Minister Sylvia Jones, said vaginal estrogen products identified by the Canadian Menopause Society, including a vaginal ring, a tablet, and inserts, are still covered on the provincial drug formulary. She said the Canadian Pharmacists Association has developed a resource for health care providers to manage supply changes. Ramesh said people who rely on the cream may face additional out-of-pocket costs and may have to move to a product that does not match their symptoms, preferences, and needs. Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-menopause-experts-raise-concerns-after-pfizer-discontinues-premarin/)

episodes.episode_title: Ep 53: Four million dollars is what one Calgary board says a new flag rule would cost its schools.
episodes.content:
# Omni View North America
> **Four million dollars is what one Calgary board says a new flag rule would cost its schools.**

**What You Need to Know:** Alberta is moving to revise a January 2027 school flag rule after boards said separate outdoor flagpoles would cost millions, including about four million dollars at the Calgary Board of Education. In Ottawa, the Liberals’ 2026 budget has passed the House. In New York, the mayor set a 2032 target to end incarceration at Rikers Island.

### Lead
**Alberta government to revise policy as school boards say new flag regulations could cost millions of dollars: CBC**
Alberta is preparing to revise new school flag regulations after education officials warned that compliance could place millions of dollars in added expenses on school boards, CBC and the Philippine Canadian Inquirer report. The regulation is scheduled to take effect in January 2027. It requires public schools to display both the Canadian flag and the Alberta flag outdoors, on separate flagpoles. Several divisions say many campuses have only one existing pole, so they would have to buy and install another. The Calgary Board of Education estimates it would need 223 additional flagpoles, with installation costs reaching approximately four million dollars. The Calgary Catholic School District expects to require another 122 poles, and it estimates each installation at between 20,000 and 30,000 dollars. Edmonton Public Schools reported that more than 170 school sites would need additional flagpoles. Edmonton Catholic Schools identified 77 locations requiring the same upgrades. Education and Childcare Minister Demetrios Nicolaides says the province is reviewing the regulation to prevent school divisions from shouldering unnecessary expenses. He has advised boards to hold off, for now, on purchasing new flagpoles while the government works on revised guidelines. One possible adjustment would let schools display both flags indoors instead of requiring separate outdoor poles. The Alberta School Boards Association called on the province to suspend the regulation, citing the financial burden and the need to preserve local decision-making. Premier Danielle Smith acknowledged that the government had not anticipated how many schools operated with only one flagpole. Opposition NDP representatives questioned the consultation process, arguing that education officials and school boards should have been involved before the policy was introduced. The proposed changes come as the new display rules also restrict which other flags may be shown on school grounds, particularly those considered to carry political or ideological messages. Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/edmonton/alberta-school-flag-regulations-costs-flagpoles-9.7427520) Source: [canadianinquirer.net](https://canadianinquirer.net/2026/11/20/alberta-to-revise-school-flag-rules-after-boards-warn-of-millions-in-added-costs/)

### Across the Region
**Liberals’ 2026 budget passes in House of Commons: Global News**
The Liberals’ 2026 budget has passed in the House of Commons, Global News reports. The budget was tabled on November 5. Global News says it outlined billions of dollars in new borrowing and tax measures. Those measures are largely aimed at stimulating infrastructure construction and other capital projects. Passage in the House is the result Global News reports today; the account does not describe a Senate vote. Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12158925/budget-2026-passes/)

**‘Multiple trade issues’ outstanding in Canada, U.S. trade talks: Sources: Global News**
Sources present at a meeting in China between Prime Minister Mark Carney and Donald Trump say multiple trade issues remain outstanding between Canada and the United States, Global News reports. Those sources say the biggest trade issue is the 25 percent U.S. tariff on Canadian automobiles. The account attributes that ranking to people who were in the room, not to a joint communiqué. The tariff figure is the concrete number those sources put on the largest unresolved item. Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12158821/canada-us-trade-talks-outstanding-issues/)

**Zohran Mamdani unveils plan to close Rikers Island jail complex: The Guardian**
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Friday unveiled a plan to close the Rikers Island jail complex, The Guardian reports. The stated goal is to end all incarceration at the current facility and relocate its remaining jail population to smaller facilities across four boroughs by the end of 2032. Mamdani said, “It is time to finally close Rikers Island.” He said New Yorkers have for decades demanded a correctional system that is safe and humane, and that the plan puts the city on a path to deliver that. He said the plan would close Rikers, reduce pretrial detention, tackle case delays that deprive people of a right to a speedy trial, and invest 146 million dollars in supports he called evidence-based and said help break cycles of incarceration. NPR reports that city officials are moving forward with plans to close Rikers, the city’s main jail complex, after years of discussion. NPR says the jail has been plagued by assaults and inmate deaths. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/20/rikers-island-closure-plan-mamdani) Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/20/nx-s1-5981356/new-york-city-rikers-jail-plans-germany-prison-model)

### The Closer Look
**California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state: The Guardian**
Coastal communities in California spent this week under hazard warnings as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves, The Guardian reports. Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued throughout the week. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into the coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights greater than 30 feet, or 9 metres, last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1 feet. The Guardian says that reading would make it the highest there in 30 years. Coastal warnings that began last weekend extended through this week, with alerts running until Friday night. For San Luis Obispo County beaches and Santa Barbara County central-coast beaches, waves of 10 to 18 feet are expected, with local sets of 18 to 22 feet.

The Guardian links those swells to the same Pacific storm systems now bringing unsettled conditions across the western United States: heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. San Francisco already saw what The Guardian calls record-breaking rainfall on Wednesday. Heavy rain also caused 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure is expected to bring considerable moisture to southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100 millimetres, or 4 inches, of rain is expected in places. Further snowfall is expected for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada.

For people on the coast, the week changed physical access and hazard status. Beaches and piers closed last weekend. Alerts were still set to run into Friday night. Another round of 10-to-18-foot waves, with local sets up to 22 feet, is forecast for San Luis Obispo County beaches and Santa Barbara County’s central coast. Inland, the same systems have already meant a Wednesday of record rain in San Francisco, as The Guardian describes it, and a power cut affecting 32,000 Sacramento customers. Through Sunday night, the forecast The Guardian cites still has more than 100 millimetres of rain in places in southern Oregon and northern California, plus more snow at Donner Pass. The account ends on those Friday-night alerts and that Sunday-night rain and snow forecast. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/20/california-coastal-communities-alert-big-waves-hit-state)

### Also Today
**Canada looks to break Starlink's grip on Arctic military communications: CBC**
CBC reports that Dominion Dynamics has signed a 2.2-million-dollar deal with Telesat to develop Arctic-ready technology, part of a broader effort to strengthen Canadian sovereignty, develop an uncrewed combat aircraft, and challenge Elon Musk’s Starlink on military satellite communications, while Advanced Television reports the prime minister saying nations should be cautious over Starlink. Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/canada-arctic-starlink-musk-satellites-9.7428908?cmp=rss) Source: [advanced-television.com](https://www.advanced-television.com/2026/11/20/canada-pm-nations-should-be-cautious-over-starlink/)

**Senate Passes Sweeping Energy Permitting Reform Bill in 62-33 Vote: OilPrice.com**
OilPrice reports the Senate has now passed a sweeping energy permitting reform bill by 62 votes to 33, a result the New York Times and WKMG describe as a measure to speed energy-project reviews and to force data centers to pay for their energy costs. Source: [oilprice.com](https://oilprice.com/Latest-Energy-News/World-News/Senate-Passes-Sweeping-Energy-Permitting-Reform-Bill-in-62-33-Vote.html) Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/19/climate/senate-passes-baaja-permitting-bill-energy.html) Source: [clickorlando.com](https://www.clickorlando.com/news/politics/2026/11/20/senate-to-vote-on-bill-to-speed-up-permitting-reviews-force-data-centers-to-pay-for-energy-costs/)

**New Ph.D. Enrollment in the Sciences Dropped 10 Percent Under Trump: The New York Times**
The New York Times reports that new Ph.D. enrollment in the sciences dropped 10 percent, that falling international enrollment drove most of the decline, and that fewer American students also started doctoral programs in 2025. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/20/us/phd-enrollment-sciences-declines.html)

**Justice Department Gives Up on Alaska Senate Lawsuit: The New York Times**
The New York Times reports that the Justice Department has given up a Trump administration lawsuit that sought to block certification of Alaska’s Senate election results if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan lost narrowly, a suit critics had called meritless. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/19/us/politics/justice-department-gives-up-on-alaska-senate-lawsuit.html)

**Raskin warns federal agencies against Signal use: The Hill**
The Hill reports that Representative Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, wrote on Thursday to a host of federal agencies, including Justice Department components and Department of Homeland Security offices, warning that apps such as Signal with auto-deleting messages violate the law and could undermine congressional oversight. episodes.episode_title: Ep 54: Ten thousand new immigration officers face training gaps called a catastrophic failure.
episodes.content:
# Omni View North America

> **Ten thousand new immigration officers face training gaps called a catastrophic failure.**

**What You Need to Know:** A draft Department of Homeland Security inspector general report finds widespread training gaps as the department sought to hire and deploy ten thousand new immigration officers, and one instructor called the regimen a catastrophic failure. A Friday executive order tells every federal contractor to notify the White House before answering Congress. The Fifth Circuit has halted a pregnant workers’ protection law because it was passed with proxy voting during the Covid pandemic.

### Lead
**Draft report finds catastrophic training failures as ICE hiring surged: The New York Times**
Officials found widespread training gaps in a draft report as the Department of Homeland Security sought to rapidly hire and deploy 10,000 new officers for the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, The New York Times reports. A draft copy of a Department of Homeland Security inspector general’s report, obtained by the Times, says the administration graduated thousands of new Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers through a training regimen one instructor called a “catastrophic failure.” The Times’ immigration reporter Hamed Aleaziz explains the draft in a separate video account of the same findings. The report is described as a draft, not a finished inspector general conclusion. The hiring target is a rapid field deployment of those 10,000 new officers. The instructor’s phrase, “catastrophic failure,” is attached in the draft account to the training regimen used to graduate the new officers. The gaps are presented as a cascade of problems found while that surge was underway. The two Times accounts — the written report and the video — describe the same draft and the same hiring surge. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/20/us/politics/training-ice-immigration-inspector-general.html) Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/video/us/100000011291007/leaked-draft-report-finds-catastrophic-training-failures-at-ice.html)

### Across the Region
**Federal court halts pregnant workers’ protection law: The New York Times**
The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals said a pregnant workers’ protection law was unconstitutional because it was passed with proxy voting during the Covid pandemic, The New York Times reports. The court halted the law. The Washington Post reports the same appeals-court holding: the pandemic-era law was passed unconstitutionally because of proxy voting. The Times says the ruling is expected to be appealed to the Supreme Court. The constitutional defect the court named is the method of passage, proxy voting in the pandemic, not a finding about the substance of workplace protections. The halt is a court result; the expected Supreme Court appeal is what the Times says comes next, not a filing the articles date. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/21/us/politics/federal-court-halts-pregnant-workers-protection-law.html) Source: [washingtonpost.com](https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/21/pandemic-era-law-passed-unconstitutionally-because-proxy-voting-appeals-court-rules/)

**Allies buy Canadian underwater drones while Canada is not there yet: CBC**
Canada has a three-ocean coastline of 243,000 kilometres and only 20 underwater drones to help defend it, CBC reports. The navy’s commander confirms there is not a solution ready. That confirmation comes a year after an internal document shows top officials talked about the need for a short-term fix. Allies are buying Canadian underwater surveillance drones. CBC’s account puts Canada’s own position in the commander’s words and in the headline phrase: Canada is “not there yet.” The gap the story measures is between a 243,000-kilometre coastline and a fleet of 20 underwater drones, with no ready solution a year after officials discussed a short-term fix. Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/canada-surveillance-gap-underwater-drone-technology-9.7425421?cmp=rss)

**Stellantis would owe Ottawa $831 million if Brampton sale proceeds: CBC**
A source told CBC that Stellantis would owe the federal government $831 million if a sale of the Brampton, Ontario, plant proceeds. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said the automaker can either keep the Brampton plant open or face a multimillion-dollar lawsuit from the federal government, Global News reports. Ontario Premier Doug Ford called the meeting “challenging” but “productive.” The $831 million figure is what a source told CBC would be owed if the sale proceeds; it is not described as money already paid. Joly’s alternative, as Global News reports it, is keep the plant open or face that federal lawsuit. Ford’s description applies to the meeting, not to a signed agreement. Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/joly-ford-stellantis-brampton-unifor-meeting-9.7430142) Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12160415/stellantis-brampton-plant-meeting-doug-ford/)

### The Closer Look
**Contractors must tell the White House first: theunionstar.com**
President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Friday that tells every federal contractor to notify the White House before answering Congress. The order, Executive Order 14438, was signed on 20 November. It says that anything the White House considers protected by executive privilege is not to be shared without its say-so.

Under the order, contractors must “NOTIFY FIRST,” informing the White House and their contracting agencies about relevant requests from Congress, and must follow “WITHHOLDING INSTRUCTIONS” for communications deemed protected by executive privilege. The order establishes “NO UNCOORDINATED DISCLOSURES” as United States policy. The requirements apply to subcontractors working on federal contracts as well. The duty is notice before an answer, not a ban on Congress asking. The withholding rule is limited, in the order’s own terms as reported, to communications the White House considers protected by executive privilege.

The White House said the order was issued on Friday. An explainer of its terms notes that the Office of Management and Budget will issue guidance on how it works in practice. Noncompliance could trigger termination of the contract, debarment or suspension. Implementation remains subject to applicable law and available appropriations, which the account of the order describes as the order’s own acknowledgement that it cannot override statutes or the Constitution. The appropriations clause is the order’s limit on itself, as that account reads it.

The order sits on the fault line between Congress and the presidency. Congress’s power to investigate the executive branch depends on getting information from the people who do the government’s work, and a large share of that work is done by contractors. What the order does not spell out in the material published so far is who decides, and how quickly, whether a given document is protected. That question is where the account says the fights will happen.

NewsBytes reports the same Friday order: contractors must clear congressional disclosures with the White House. Traders Union reports that the White House expanded oversight limits for federal contractors. The three accounts describe one action — Friday’s order putting the White House and contracting agencies in front of a contractor’s answer to Congress — and the fullest terms are the ones theunionstar.com publishes: Executive Order 14438, signed 20 November, notice first, withholding instructions, no uncoordinated disclosures, subcontractors included, and penalties of termination, debarment or suspension, subject to law and appropriations. Source: [theunionstar.com](https://www.theunionstar.com/contractors-must-tell-white-house-first-trump-signs-order-on-congressional-requests/) Source: [newsbytesapp.com](https://www.newsbytesapp.com/news/world/trump-orders-contractors-to-clear-congress-disclosures-with-white-house/tldr) Source: [tradersunion.com](https://tradersunion.com/news/companies/show/4355237-white-house-federal-contractors-oversight/)

### Also Today

NPR reports that a national effort to ensure that only winners of the popular vote become president could reach a critical milestone soon, though hurdles remain. Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/21/nx-s1-6044237/electoral-college-national-popular-vote-interstate-compact)

An arbitration ruling gives British Columbia nurses 3 percent annual wage increases through 2029, after they asked for 8 percent a year, and the union president says the decision left nurses feeling “gravely disappointed.” Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-bc-nurses-get-3-annual-wage-increases-through-2029-in-arbitration/)

The Parti Québécois government pledged to unveil a road map for phasing out fossil fuels, and environmental groups praised the commitment, The Globe and Mail reports. **Tenants ordered to vacate Edmonton apartment building: Global News**
Stadium Plaza tenants in central Edmonton were released from their leases and ordered to vacate a building Global News describes as overrun by squatters and without heat after copper pipe theft. Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12160420/edmonton-stadium-plaza-eviction/)

A senior Democrat in the U.S. Senate said Canada should seek an interim trade deal with the Trump administration and that the incoming Congress will figure out something better for the long term, CBC reports. **Jury finds man guilty of arson in Palisades Fire: The New York Times**
A jury found Jonathan Rinderknecht guilty on two counts in the Palisades Fire trial, The New York Times reports, in a verdict the paper says provides a measure of accountability for a painful chapter in recent Los Angeles history. The Chinese Embassy in Mexico slammed a U.S. consul general’s claims about Chinese investment near the border and urged an end to interference, Global Times reports. Source: [globaltimes.cn](https://www.globaltimes.cn/page/202611/1374758.shtml)

Baja California is expanding industrial parks to boost cross-border supply chains and attract foreign investment, the Imperial Valley Press reports from Mexicali. episodes.episode_title: Ep 55: Bayer's Roundup settlement could cost billions for thousands with a linked blood cancer.
episodes.content:
# Omni View North America
> **Bayer's Roundup settlement could cost billions for thousands with a linked blood cancer.**

**What You Need to Know:** Bayer has reached a Roundup settlement that could cost the company billions, with the money going to thousands of people who have been or will be diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma, a blood cancer NPR links to the herbicide. A federal judge in Rhode Island has blocked a Trump administration effort to shift homelessness aid from housing subsidies toward treatment for mental illness and addiction. Ontario Liberals have elected Navdeep Bains to lead a party rebuilding after three straight election losses, while Ottawa's press dinner put the Canada–US trade fight back in public view.

### Lead
**Bayer reaches Roundup settlement that could cost the company billions: NPR**
NPR reports that Bayer has reached a Roundup settlement that could cost the company billions. The money will go to thousands of people who have been diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma or who will be diagnosed with it. NPR describes that illness as a blood cancer linked to the herbicide. The people covered are not limited to those already diagnosed; the report says the money is also for people who will be diagnosed. NPR presents the settlement as the result now on the record. It does not, in the account used here, describe a new trial verdict sitting beside that settlement. What changes is the path for those thousands: payment is tied to the settlement NPR reports, and the cost to Bayer is framed as one that could run to billions. The herbicide at the center of the claims is Roundup. Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/21/nx-s1-6049684/roundup-bayer-hodgkins-settlement)

### Across the Region
**Ontario Liberals choose Navdeep Bains as new leader: The Globe and Mail**
Navdeep Bains has been elected leader of Ontario's Liberal Party, The Globe and Mail reports. The Globe and Mail identifies him as a former federal cabinet minister. He fended off Lee Fairclough, whom the paper describes as a stiff challenge. The party is looking to rebuild after three consecutive election losses. CBC reports that insiders say Bains faces a serious challenge rebuilding Ontario's Liberal party. The election of a leader is a completed party result, not a forecast of the next provincial vote. Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-ontario-liberal-party-new-leader-navdeep-bains/) Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/toronto/navdeep-bains-liberal-leader-9.7431590) Source: [hindustantimes.com](https://www.hindustantimes.com/world-news/indocanadian-and-trudeau-ally-navdeep-bains-elected-ontario-liberal-leader-canada-101795328905133.html)

**Judge Blocks Trump Administration’s Effort to Transform Homelessness Policy: The New York Times**
A federal judge in Rhode Island has blocked the Trump administration’s effort to transform homelessness policy, The New York Times reports. The paper calls the decision a blow to an effort to shift aid away from housing subsidies. The shift the administration had pursued would have favored treatment for mental illness and addiction instead. The ruling stops that shift from going forward on the terms the administration had pursued. The actor is a federal judge in Rhode Island, and the policy under challenge is the administration’s homelessness-aid approach. People who receive housing subsidies are the ones the blocked shift would have moved away from, toward treatment-centered aid, according to the Times account. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/21/us/politics/judge-trump-homeless-aid-addiction-treatment.html)

**The Penny Is Dead. Now It’s Official.: The New York Times**
President Trump signed a law on Friday formally putting the penny out of mint, The New York Times reports. The coin had already stopped being struck a year earlier. Friday’s signature is the formal end of minting, not the day the presses first went quiet. The Times presents the signing as making that earlier stop official. Anyone still using pennies already in circulation is not told, in this account, that existing coins were pulled. What changed on Friday is the legal status of further minting. Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/21/us/politics/penny-mint-trump-common-cent-act.html)

### The Closer Look
**‘He got a great a**’: Trump impersonator’s cheeky joke leaves Mark Carney in splits: WION**
At Ottawa’s annual Parliamentary Press Gallery Dinner on Saturday, a Donald Trump impersonator performed beside Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and left him laughing, WION reports. Pretending to be the US president, the performer joked about having two Carneys on stage and described the Canadian leader as “almost as popular as me.” An explicit remark about Carney’s backside drew particular attention; the impersonator called it “incredible” and “beautiful,” then mimicked what WION calls Trump’s signature firm handshake. The same set turned to the trade fight. The performer joked about getting a deal done “before the nukes,” described himself as “crazy,” and said he was looking for an ambassador “less likeable than me.” He delivered the line “He puts the ass in ambassador,” and joked that he would reject press-secretary candidates who were “too smart.” On the Canada–US trade war, WION quotes him: “We’re gonna have a great deal. There’s only one thing standing in the way – me, because I’m crazy, but that’s ok.”

Carney used the same dinner to answer in kind. “This is a tough room. And I've been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator,” he said, drawing laughter, in a reference to the US president’s revamp of the Oval Office and his taste for elaborate decor. He also said he was prepared to work with “anyone—ideologues, tyrants, dictators,” and described that approach as “cooperative federalism.” Those lines are jokes at a press dinner, attributed by WION to Carney, not a new statute.

WION places the laughter against a feud it says has run for the past year, with Canada and the United States locked in a bitter trade dispute. Trade talks between the two countries collapsed in September, WION reports. Trump imposed 50 per cent tariffs on imports from Canada. Ottawa retaliated with what it described as “dollar for dollar” tariffs on American goods, which WION says further worsened relations. The people on the receiving end of that tariff pair are importers and exporters on both sides of the border: American goods faced Ottawa’s matching tariffs, and Canadian imports faced the 50 per cent US rate WION attributes to Trump. The dinner did not, in this account, restart the talks that collapsed in September. It put the collapsed talks, the tariff rates, and each leader’s public posture in the same room, with Carney speaking for himself and the impersonator speaking only as a performer. Source: [wionews.com](https://www.wionews.com/trending/he-got-a-great-a-trump-impersonator-s-cheeky-joke-leaves-mark-carney-in-splits-video-1795341302033)

### Also Today

episodes.content:
# Omni View North America
> **Ten point eight percent of Canadian men aged twenty-five to thirty-four use cannabis daily, above alcohol.**

**What You Need to Know:** A Canadian Medical Association Journal study finds daily cannabis use is more common than daily alcohol among adults, and highest among men 25 to 34 at 10.8 percent. The Democratic National Committee has set 12 primary debates for 2028, with the first in June 2027. In Newfoundland, a Memorial University paper reports forever-chemical levels in surface foam far above Health Canada’s drinking-water guideline, as residents sue Ottawa.

### Lead
**Daily cannabis use more common among Canadian adults than daily alcohol consumption, study finds: The Globe and Mail**
A study in the Canadian Medical Association Journal, released Monday, finds daily cannabis use is more common than daily alcohol use among Canadian adults, and equals or exceeds daily cigarette use among people younger than 35. Researchers used the 2023-2024 Canadian Community Health Survey, covering nearly 100,000 people age 18 and older. Among men aged 25 to 34, daily cannabis use was 10.8 percent, against 2.9 percent for daily alcohol and 8 percent for cigarettes; among women in that age group the figures were 6.8 percent, 1.2 percent and 4.5 percent. Among women 18 to 24, daily cannabis use was 6.6 percent, daily alcohol 0.4 percent and daily cigarettes 2 percent, with similar patterns among men in that age group. Lead author André McDonald, a psychiatric epidemiologist and Canadian Institutes of Health Research postdoctoral fellow at McMaster University’s Peter Boris Centre for Addictions Research, said the results suggest a generational shift with long-term implications for population health. Senior author Daniel Myran, the Cheesbrough research chair at North York General Hospital, said many daily cannabis users do not drink or smoke cigarettes every day; three in five reported no concurrent daily cigarette use, nine in ten reported no concurrent daily alcohol use, and 68 percent of daily users smoke cannabis. The work, funded through a Terry Fox Research Institute award to Dr. Myran, comes eight years after Canada in October 2018 became the first major industrialized nation to legalize non-medical cannabis; the authors cite risks including psychosis and schizophrenia and say further research is needed because a significant share of daily users started after legalization. **High levels of toxic forever chemicals found near Newfoundland site, study finds: The Globe and Mail**
More than two decades after firefighters last sprayed flame-dousing foam at a Newfoundland practice facility, a Memorial University paper published earlier this month in Environmental Science & Technology finds high concentrations of toxic forever chemicals still turning up several kilometres away. The work appears to bolster residents living downstream of St. John’s International Airport who are suing the federal government, alleging the chemicals have fouled their drinking water. Ed Sheerr, a lead plaintiff in a proposed class action for roughly 700 households, said the contamination researchers found was significantly more widespread than the plaintiffs had recognized. The lawsuit argues that per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances from the airport training facility have contaminated local well water, imperiling health and cratering property values, and it asks for immediate remediation and compensation.

Memorial researchers began sampling in December 2024 after learning Transport Canada was not testing private wells outside a designated subdivision near the airport where PFAS had been found. Karl Jobst, a Memorial chemistry professor, said the team, led by PhD student Emmanuel Tolefe, wanted to understand the spread and offer free testing. The highest readings were in foams that form on surface waters near the airport, reaching 2,000,000 nanograms per litre, against a Health Canada drinking-water guideline of 30 nanograms per litre. Water samples near the airport ranged from 318 to 2,302 nanograms per litre. Levels fell with distance but stayed above the drinking-water standard more than four kilometres away. Researchers detected the chemicals in 32 of 42 private wells sampled, and in seven of those wells the levels exceeded the guideline. PFOS, a major component of foams used at the airport between 1982 and 2004, made up 62 percent of the PFAS detected near the defunct practice facility. The paper describes PFAS as a family of more than 6,000 synthetic chemicals, linked in recent years to kidney and testicular cancer, metabolic disruption, immune suppression, pregnancy complications and other harms.

Transport Canada has acknowledged using PFAS-laden foams. In its statement of defence it denies that any PFAS migrated from the airport to drinking-water wells, and spokesperson Sau Sau Liu said the department will not comment on the paper because of the proposed class action. The agency is delivering bottled water to Mr. Sheerr and other residents whose water exceeds the Health Canada threshold. A Globe and Mail analysis last year found eight communities across six provinces in a similar position, relying on federal bottled water, and Ottawa has identified 86 federal properties where PFAS has fouled groundwater. Mr. Sheerr said he hopes the study will push the government to work with residents rather than deny responsibility. The fine print is still being worked out, and the agreements are expected to be ratified next year. Goods exports to the 11 ASEAN countries doubled over the past decade to 11.6 billion dollars in 2025, while imports nearly tripled to 41 billion dollars — 1.5 percent of Canadian merchandise exports and 5.2 percent of imports. Mr. Carney said the Philippines deal, which would give preferential tariff treatment to 97 percent of Canadian products, could triple exports over the next decade from 1 billion dollars in 2025, led by pork, wheat and wood products; a 2017 Global Affairs Canada feasibility report estimated an ASEAN agreement could lift Canadian exports by 2.67 billion dollars a year. Jeff Nankivell, president and chief executive of the Asia Pacific Foundation of Canada, said Canada is playing catch-up and must keep up the engagement, while Wayne Farmer, president of the Canada-ASEAN Business Council, said President Donald Trump’s pressure on Malaysia, Cambodia and Indonesia is making Canada look more appealing as a partner that does not weaponize trade. # Omni View North America
> **One hundred twenty-seven Quebec legislators must swear fealty to the King to sit.**

**What You Need to Know:** One hundred twenty-seven Quebec legislators must swear fealty to the King to sit. A court has ruled that members must take that oath after they swore allegiance only to the people of Quebec following the October 5 election, and Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has rejected the order. A ruling on the oath was expected yesterday; he has said he cannot take an oath to the King of England.

### Lead
**Quebec court rules MNAs must swear fealty to the King: The Globe and Mail**
A Quebec court has ruled that politicians must swear an oath to King Charles to sit in the National Assembly. The Globe and Mail reports that after the October 5 election, the province’s 127 legislators swore allegiance only to the people of Quebec. A decision on the oath was expected yesterday. Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has rejected the ruling that orders members to swear the oath. In CBC’s account of his response, he said, “I cannot take an oath to the King of England.” Global News reported the judge’s order as a condition of sitting. Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/politics/article-politics-insider-quebec-court-rules-mnas-must-swear-fealty-to-the-king/) Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/player/play/video/9.7433598) Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/player/play/video/9.7432811) Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/video/12163246/quebec-politicians-must-swear-an-oath-to-king-charles-to-sit-in-the-national-assembly-judge-rules)

Elections director Jeff Elrod said the official winner will not be included in what is submitted to the secretary of the Senate. Unofficial election-night totals had independent Jesse Battles at 20,341 and Republican Senator Andrew Jones of Centre at 20,289; Elrod’s totals, with provisional and write-in ballots, widened Battles’ lead. Battles has declared victory and was sworn in on November 10 by an Etowah County circuit judge after the Alabama Republican Party removed him from the primary ballot; Jones has not conceded and wrote that every vote needs to be accurately counted. Secretary of State Wes Allen said Cherokee, Etowah and DeKalb counties will recount with the electronic-voting vendor and sheriffs. Certified results in the other races, Alabama Daily News reported, solidify four seats Democrats flipped while Republicans keep a supermajority in both chambers and won every statewide contest; new constitutional officers are to be inaugurated on January 18, 2027, and the session begins February 2, 2027. ### The Closer Look
**Galloway’s lawyers say he deserves one of Canada’s largest defamation awards: The Globe and Mail**
Steven Galloway’s lawyers began closing arguments Monday in British Columbia Supreme Court, asking Justice Neena Sharma for what they call one of the largest defamation awards in Canadian history. The Globe and Mail reports they want millions from four defendants they allege ruined the bestselling author’s career by spreading sexual assault allegations.

Lead counsel Daniel Burnett asked for at least $2.5-million in general, aggravated and punitive damages from a former creative-writing student, known as A.B. under a publication ban, tied to allegations she made in 2015. Arguments continue Tuesday on special damages against A.B. alone, a claim the lawyers expect will add millions more for a decade of lost income and for future earnings they say were wiped out. Daniel Coles told the court one expert put lost income to date and earnings to age 70 at $7.1-million, and another at $11.7-million. Burnett said A.B. “orchestrated lies to support the lies,” was “tactical,” and sought “maximum damage,” causing “years of suffering.”

He asked that Mandi Gray pay at least $250,000, Glynnis Kirchmeier at least $80,000, and Dana Kagis $30,000, for posts the lawyers say repeated the claim that Galloway sexually assaulted A.B. A.B. did not testify. At the start of the trial a lawyer said she was withdrawing defences of truth and fair comment. She denies spreading lies about Galloway, with whom she had a two-year relationship. Her lawyers have told the court she tried to kill herself twice this year because of the stress of the case.

Galloway was never charged with a crime. The University of British Columbia suspended him when the allegations surfaced in November 2015. In 2016 a former Supreme Court justice hired by the university found that, on a balance of probabilities, it could not be established that he committed sexual assault or assault. She did find that he had sexually harassed A.B. and committed other misconduct, and he was dismissed that year. He sued almost two dozen defendants in 2018.

Burnett asked the judge to rule the allegations false, which he said would help restore Galloway’s reputation and would matter for Kirchmeier, who lives in the United States and, he explained, is not typically liable for a foreign ruling unless a defamatory claim is proven false. He said that in correspondence with other professors A.B. claimed CBC News had reviewed her evidence and intended to cover the story, which he said she has admitted was not the case, and that a producer for CBC’s the fifth estate was copied on her email to the university president. He argued she, Gray and Kirchmeier acted out of malice, described Gray’s posts as treating Galloway like “roadkill,” and said Kirchmeier should be penalized for blurting out in court “other bad acts” alleged by a different former student who settled with Galloway on the eve of trial.

Closing arguments continue this week from A.B.’s counsel, Gray’s lawyer, and Kirchmeier, who is attending law school and representing herself remotely. Kagis has not participated and has no representation. Some time in the new year, the court will hear a further matter concerning A.B. Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-galloways-lawyers-say-he-deserves-one-of-canadas-largest-defamation/)

# Omni View North America
> **Twenty months of court fights ended when Kilmar Abrego Garcia left for Spain, not Liberia.**

**What You Need to Know:** Twenty months of court fights ended when Kilmar Abrego Garcia left the United States for Spain rather than face the prospect of deportation to Liberia. The Pentagon is threatening further measures unless Canada puts continental defence first in its military buildup. In Ontario, two cancer patients are in court over refused funding for treatment in the United States, while private-university students remain cut off from OSAP.

### Lead
**Kilmar Abrego Garcia leaves U.S. voluntarily for Spain: NPR**
Kilmar Armando Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran immigrant, left the United States voluntarily on Tuesday for Spain. NPR reported the departure came after nearly two years of legal battles; The New York Times described it as the end of a 20-month fight. The Times reported that he was wrongfully deported last year. He left facing the prospect that the Trump administration might deport him to Liberia, the Times reported. NPR described him as a symbol of President Trump’s mass deportation campaign. The voluntary departure is the result the courts had not yet imposed: he chose Spain rather than wait on a further removal. Source: [npr.org](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/25/nx-s1-6053203/abrego-garcia-leaves-us) Source: [nytimes.com](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/24/us/politics/abrego-garcia-leave-deportation.html)

Their lawyers say Ontario changed its out-of-country health-care rules in bad faith. The case challenges a funding refusal, not a grant of treatment. Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/toronto/ontario-out-of-country-treatment-cancer-patients-court-9.7434936) Source: [theglobeandmail.com](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-ontario-changed-out-of-country-health-care-rules-in-bad-faith/)

**Politics Insider: Committee rejects major changes, sends major projects bill back to the House: The Globe and Mail**

The committee wrapped up more than 100 hours of debate over amendments that labour and environmental organizations had called for. Those organizations did not get the major changes they sought.
